recommendations.text: Legislation Texts should be drafted, adopted and implemented in order to achieve equivalence with EU legislation in the areas covered by the mission.

Laboratories The implementation of quality assurance should be completed, in particular the validation of the methods. The performance of the currently unreliable analyses should be improved. All the analyses should be performed as planned and in due time. The National Reference Laboratory should develop its tasks of technical assistance and provide for proficiency tests.

Residues The Residue Monitoring Plan should be drawn up and implemented in accordance with the requirements of the Directive 96/23/EC. Targeting criteria should be applied for sampling. In order to guarantee an adequate supervision of the distribution and use of veterinary drugs, more mandatory control tools should be implemented, such as records and registers.

Fishery products The hygiene supervision at the level of fishing vessels and landing sites should be improved. The exports of tuna to the EU should be stopped until adequate supervision, including histamine checks, of this production is performed. The results of all chemical analyses performed on fish should be collected and sent to the European Commission for evaluation. EU-approval should be granted only for the establishments that fulfil all EU requirements, and should specify the types of activities and products. Deficiencies identified in four of the five establishments visited should be rectified and the fifth one should be withdrawn from the list. The revised list of EU-approved fishery product establishments should be forwarded to all the Member States concerned and to the European Commission. 22 A model export health certificate should be drawn up in every language of Member State of destination.

Written Guarantees The Cypriot competent authority should provide the European Commission with written guarantees setting out the action that will be taken in response to the above recommendations, and the deadlines by which this action will be completed, within one month of receiving the final version of this report. 8.2. To the Commission Services ­ The Commission Services should evaluate the written assurances received from the Cypriot competent authority. ­ The assessment by the Commission of the annual residue monitoring plan should take into account the findings of the mission. ­ As regards fishery products, provided that satisfactory guarantees are received, the Commission services should propose that Cyprus be placed on the list I of Annex of the amended Commission Decision 97/296/EC and that a Commission Decision laying down the health conditions for the importation of fishery products originating in Cyprus be adopted. 23 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/1051/2000 Competent Authority response to the recommendations in the report The competent authority of Cyprus has provided written guarantees in response to the recommendations made in the report, which will be published together with the final report on the website of the Health and Consumer Protection Directorate-General. These guarantees are the following: · Legislation: Transposition of the `acquis communautaire' is on-going. In particular new legislation is being drafted in order to include the provisions of directives 91/493/EEC and 92/48/EEC, and will give all competencies to the Veterinary Services for fishery products sanitary aspects. No deadline has been given for the adoption of the new texts. Regarding residues new legislation is planned for 2001. · Laboratories Efforts are being made on the upgrading and accreditation of laboratories. Inspections for accreditation are planned in 2001 for the State General Laboratory and in 2002 for the Laboratory for the Control of Food of Animal Origin of the Veterinary Services. Some of the recommendations in the report have already been addressed. · Residues Recommendations in the report will be included in the National Residue Plan for 2001 and in the new legislation. · Fishery products Guarantees have been provided for all the recommendations. A new list of four fishery product establishments approved for export to the EU, specifying the type of products, has been set up and forwarded to the European Commission and to France. 24

To ensure that deficiencies found during this mission are addressed in all EU-approved establishments.

audits.title: Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSEs) in Sheep and Goats and Animal Nutrition

recommendations.text: To ensure that the identification and registration system for sheep and goats is able to fully support eradication measures for TSEs, as required by Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, and to consider using the information to improve prevention and eradication of the disease.

To ensure that monitoring of healthy slaughtered goats and dead on-farm sheep and goats includes animals in non-infected flocks and complies with the targets given in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To retain under official control carcasses of healthy slaughtered goats sampled to be tested for TSE until the result of the test is known, as required by chapter A of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To try to collect part of the cerebellum when samples are taken, as required by chapter C of Annex X to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, and to consider submitting positive cases to further laboratory testing if the possibility of an atypical strain of Scrapie can not be excluded.

To ensure that the NRL has enough capacity to test all samples received, particularly as regards rapid tests, in order to enable the CA to implement a TSEs monitoring programme and to allow compliance with provisions in points 7.1 and 7.3 in chapter A (II) of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 17 With regard to measures following suspicion/confirmation of TSEs
To ensure that measures provided in order to handle suspicion of TSEs in sheep and goats are always applied in line with Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001

To ensure that confirmed cases of TSEs in sheep and goats are forwarded for further laboratory testing with a primary molecular typing method in line with chapter B of Annex X to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To ensure that national provisions on eradication measures and their application are in line with requirements laid down in Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 836/2004 and in Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. With regard to breeding programmes for resistance to TSEs

To make it compulsory for all flocks to participate in the breeding programme as required by Article 2(2) of Decision 2003/100/EC and to ensure its implementation in line with requirements contained in Annex I thereto. With regard to SRM
To take steps to ensure the correct removal of SRM from carcasses destined for human consumption, as required by Annex XI to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

To ensure that the entire head and organs of the thoracic and abdominal cavities of animals slaughtered in accordance with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 836/2004 are disposed of as required by point 5 of Annex VII to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. With regard to official inspections in the field of animal nutrition

To review the cooperation agreement between the CA involved in the official inspections in the field of animal nutrition and the resources available, to ensure that the system of official controls complies fully with Article 4 of Directive 95/53/EC.

To reconsider the elements which should be included in the national control programme for animal nutrition, especially to take account of the annual EU recommendations concerning the implementation of the coordinated inspection programme in the field of animal nutrition. With regard to approval and registration of E/I
To ensure that all E/I approved or registered according to Directive 95/69/EC, meet all of the relevant requirements given in the Annex to this Directive.

To ensure that penalties imposed comply with Article 19 of Directive 95/53/EC. __________________ 18 ADDENDUM RESPONSE OF THE COMPETENT AUTHORITIES TO THE RECOMMENDATIONS Comments from the Cypriot CA on the draft report were received on 16 February 2006, and included an outline of the actions planned and/or undertaken to address certai s contained in the report. These may be summarised as follows: With regard to the control of TSE in sheep and goats 1. A report generated by the IRSC system has been prepared which enables all the contacts of a certain farm with other farms to be traced backwards and forwards. Consideration is being given to the potential role of this system in the prevention and eradication programme for Scrapie. 2. A Circular has been sent to the DVO´s, the Local Veterinary Stations and the slaughterhouses to require the collection of samples from healthy slaughtered goats aged over 18 months which come from non-infected flocks. Advice was also given on estimating the age of animals to be sampled. 3. Veterinary officers in the slaughterhouses have been instructed that no carcass of a goat subject to a rapid test is to be stamped and released for human consumption until the NRL confirms a negative test result. 4. A series of training courses concerning the correct collection of the samples has already taken place and another four courses are planned. 5. citations.text: GMO controls of feed mills are part of hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) inspections. The inspection frequency is subject to the risk profile of the company for aspects other than GMO, such as the production of medicated feed, the use of proteins of animal origin and production volume. However, the risk of GM cross-contamination in feed mills manufacturing compound feeds both with and without GMO and potential non- compliance with labelling requirements in that regard has not been covered by the CAs in the framework of official controls (see also paragraph 45 below).

Controls for GMOs in feed do not verify compliance with labelling requirements in relation to potential cross-contamination. Therefore official controls can overlook that such requirements are not implemented by feed business operators.

As stated by the feed mill, they carry out flushing of the production lines when producing different products, however, the company has never assessed that this flushing procedure was effective in preventing the risk of cross-contamination with GMOs. This is not in line with Article 24(3) of Regulation (EC) 1829/2003 which requires that operators take appropriate steps to avoid the presence of GMOs in non-GM products. citations.text: Farmers in Cyprus are required to keep an inventory of medicinal products purchased and used. Such inventories were kept at the farms visited, but contrary to the requirements in EU legislation 49 (where keepers of food-producing animals need to maintain treatment records for a period of five years after the treatment), the registration of use of veterinary medicinal products (treatment records) presented deficiencies as follows: at the dairy farm the treatment records detailed the individual animals, the dates and the withdrawal periods. Withdrawal periods for milk were reflected in days, and did not permit a verification of whether the cow was excluded from commercial production for a sufficient number of milkings (withdrawal periods should be indicated in whole days, except for milk withdrawal periods, which may be more appropriately expressed in whole hours 50). The farmer stated that he always extended the withdrawal period by two days but this was not reflected in the records. at the pig farm, the farmer applied routine prophylactic treatments for the different age groups, through feed. Injectable medicines were in stock and the farmer confirmed that they were used when necessary. There were no records of these treatments. at the poultry farm, routine treatments of antibiotics used as prophylaxis after vaccinations were recorded for every shed, but the use of colistin (that had been prescribed by a veterinarian) was not recorded and could not be traced to any batch of animals (the prescription did not include this information). 48 Article 67 of Directive 2001/82/EC. 49 Directive 96/23/EC (Article 10), Directive 2001/82/EC (Article 69) and Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 (Annex I, Part A, III, 8(b)). 50 https://ec.europa.eu/health/sites/health/files/files/eudralex/vol-6/c/spcpharmaceuticals_10-07- 2006_en.pdf 15 At the aquaculture farm some treatments were recorded but the treatment with malachite green (see finding 32) that had led to the detection of residues in food had not been recorded. recommendations.text: To ensure that documented procedures cover all relevant areas of controls along the production chain of bovine meat, as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In particular, the Veterinary Services should provide the control staff involved in official controls of bovine slaughterhouses with adequate documented procedures in order to be able to act appropriately in case of bovine animals with traceability issues.

citations.text: While the audit team did not carry out a comprehensive review of these guidelines, it was noted that they cover all of the food chain and controls related to the production of beef. However, the audit team noted that the "Instruction on procedures to be followed in slaughterhouses" does not provide sufficient information for the OVs on how to act appropriately in case of bovine animals with traceability issues (e.g. lost ear tags) detected at AMI. This has a negative impact on the official controls on bovine traceability. (See also paragraphs 79 and 81).

The CAs have issued national legislation and guidelines necessary to ensure the implementation and/or enforcement of EU requirements applicable to the bovine meat sector. From a summary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation and mostly adequate, with the exception of those dealing with cases of bovine animals with traceability issues. 3

As part of the AMI, the OV verifies the identification of animals in the bovine database (see paragraph 72). If any non-compliances are detected in relation to the traceability of animals, the OV should follow the procedures laid down in the relevant VS instruction (see paragraph 4). The audit team noted that this instruction refers to the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1053/2010, which requires that if the keeper of an animal cannot prove its identification and traceability, the CA shall, where appropriate, on the basis of an assessment of the animal health and food safety risks, order the destruction of the animal without compensation.

One of the OVs interviewed explained that where the traceability of a bovine animal is not established (e.g. lost ear tag(s)), it will be slaughtered and the carcass will be detained and tested for antibiotic residues. If the result of the analysis is negative, the meat is declared fit for human consumption. The audit team noted that these actions were the initiatives of the OV, as they are not included in the VS instruction. The audit team was provided with examples of such cases and noted that a 400 fine was imposed on the farmers in each case.

In addition, the audit team reviewed a case when a bovine animal arrived at the slaughterhouse with one ear tag. After verification of the identification of this animal in the CBD, the OV ascertained that this ear tag belonged to an animal which, according to the data in the CBD, had already been declared dead. Despite the fact that the traceability of this animal was clearly not established, its meat was released for human consumption by the OV. The CA imposed a 400 fine on the farmer. A representative from the VPHD informed the audit team that the procedure included in the instruction does not provide sufficient information to direct OVs to act appropriately in such situations and that the VS plan to revise this instruction (see also paragraph 79).

citations.text: The VPHD inspectors collect official samples to verify the reliability of results obtained by operators in their own-checks programmes. The VS designated official laboratory carries out analyses for microbiological standards, and uses official laboratory located in another Member State for carrying out analyses for glyceroltriheptanoate (GTH) content. The audit team noted that: a. Both laboratories analysing official samples are accredited to ISO 17025. The VS laboratory has the methods used for analyses of official samples within the scope of its accreditation. The laboratory from the other Member State does not. The latter is not in line with Article 37(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The VPHD representative stated that the external laboratory in question regularly participates in the inter-laboratory tests organised by the EU Reference Laboratory for detection and quantification of GTH, with successful outcomes. Nonetheless, in response to this finding, during this audit, the VS representatives declared they would seek a laboratory with an accredited method for GTH. b. Despite the absence of written guidelines on official sampling explaining `what', `where' and `how' to sample, official samples were properly targeted to relevant operators (processing Category 1 and Category 2 material) and properly reflected the scope of examination (GTH content and microbiological standards). c. In 2019 and 2020, with some exceptions, inspectors collected all of the planned samples. Exceptions concerned a few situations resulting from COVID-19 related restrictions and cases where operators had suspended or ceased their activity. d. The sampling protocols and results of laboratory analyses contained a unique serial number. The VPHD inspectors stated that they record the number in DVO (5) sampling logs and put it on a disposable bag (sealed with tamperproof seal) containing the sample. The number allows linking the sample, the place of sampling and examination result, thus ensuring legal, scientific and technical validity required by Article 34(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Whilst official samples were collected and tested as planned in accredited official laboratories, the fact that one of the designated laboratories does not have the analytical method used for GTH analysis included in the scope of its accreditation as required by EU law, may compromise the competent authority in taking enforcement action in the event of a non-compliant result being found.

citations.text: Following the first confirmed finding of S. frugiperda in January 2023, the CA did not immediately establish a demarcated area, as the first finding was found in a light trap on the property of a private citizen and was not associated with a growing crop or located near host species. However, the CA did carry out intensive surveys assisted by trapping to detect the pest in the vicinity of the outbreak, in accordance with the action plan.

In July 2023, the second finding occurred, where one S. frugiperda larva was detected in a maize crop in Larnaca district and then again in September 2023, the CA reported the third official detection of the pest in a maize crop in Nicosia. According to the first Europhyt update (ref: 01/2023-07-26) on the outbreak, the CA stated that they demarcated a 100 m infested area and a 100 km buffer zone around the outbreak site, and in effect demarcating the entire island. Contrary to the Europhyt update, the audit team noted during the site visits, that the infested zones were considered to be the field or plot of land where the infestation occurred but did not include a radius of 100 m around the infestation. Furthermore, host plants such as potatoes and brassicas growing in plots immediately adjacent to the infested ones or within the 100 m radius, were not included in the infested zone (see paragraph 22 and 27). This is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2023/11345, requiring that the infested zone is to include the infested plants and all plants which are liable to become infested within a 100 m radius around the finding of S. frugiperda.

According to the CA, maize, peppers and aubergines are considered to be a risk among those specified plants referred to in Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/638, which was in force up until 30 June 2023. citations.text: Following the first finding of S. frugiperda, the CA conducted intensive surveys with the assistance of trapping in the vicinity of this finding, focusing their efforts on production sites of host plants of maize, peppers and aubergines considered to be a risk for the presence of the pest (see paragraph 22). However, according to the EFSA pest survey card, delimiting surveys should cover all host species in the survey area. Surveys are not carried out in line with Articles 19(1) and 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, which requires that surveys shall take account of scientific and technical evidence, and any other appropriate information, concerning the presence of the pests concerned.

At the time of the second finding in a maize crop, Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 applied, with regards to the requirements for surveys in demarcated areas. According to the action plan of 14 March 2023, surveillance and sampling for the presence of S. frugiperda, a mix of seven funnel and delta pheromone traps were to be placed within the 5 km buffer zone. These were checked once or twice a week, 11 respectively, and the insect samples were sent to the PPL for analysis. In the update to the action plan (12 September 2023), it provided instructions for the placement of a further 17 funnel and delta traps in the Nicosia, Limassol, Larnaca, and the Paphos areas, which were to be checked every 15 days.

On 12 June 2023, Annex 1 to Regulation (EU) 2023/1134, provided an extended list of host plants, including certain Solanum spp. and Brassicaceae. However, following the second finding of the pest, the CA maintained their survey focus on the three crops referred to in paragraph 27, without full consideration for the other hosts listed in the annex to the above Regulation or the EFSA pest survey card. This is not fully in line with Article 7(b) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134, which requires scouting in sites of production where host plants are grown.

In the update to the action plan (12 September 2023) when Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 applied, there was no survey design or sampling scheme developed, which should provide guidelines on being able to identify with at least a 95 % level of confidence, a 1 % a level of presence of the specified pest. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 7(c) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134.

citations.text: The CA carries out regular surveys in the demarcated areas for D. citri in parallel with the survey for C. Liberibacter. These surveys are focused on production sites of citrus fruit, nurseries and garden centres with host plants including citrus and Murraya spp. plants. However, as a result of the buffer zone not being clearly defined (see paragraphs 23 and 24), these surveys were conducted all over Cyprus.

The audit team noted that citrus trees were abundant all over Cyprus however, abandoned orchards, private properties and urban areas with bitter orange (Citrus aurantium) trees growing on the footpaths, are not included in the scope of the survey. According to the CA, this was due to the lack of resources. Furthermore, the CA requires permission to access private properties and if refused it would require a court order to gain access, which was too complicated, so it was not done. This is not in line with Articles 19(1) and 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, which requires that the survey shall be carried out in all appropriate locations and be based on sound scientific and technical principles.

The ADO staff informed the audit team that surveys are in general based on visual examination of plant material of trees grown in orchards, for detecting symptoms caused by D. citri adults or nymphs. They also stated that as a result of the information 12 campaign raised by the Department of Agriculture for D. citri, the producers frequently report suspicious symptoms concerning its presence.

ADO staff have been instructed to focus the survey on citrus trees in places of production at the time of new flushing, in spring, mid-summer and late autumn. The ADO staff follow an "S-shape" course within the citrus orchards and focus on the recently developed flushes of young stems and leaves of trees. However, this is not always possible, in particular for the developing upper parts of the tree canopy and surveillance efforts are mostly limited to leaves growing within the lower interior central part of the trees.

According to the statement of the ADOs staff, one yellow sticky trap is deployed per citrus orchard regardless of its size. However, out of the six citrus orchards visited, only one yellow sticky trap was spotted by the audit team in an orchard located in the Asomatos Limassol area where the presence of D. citri was first reported. Also, in the nurseries and garden centres visited, close to infested zones, the audit team noted that yellow sticky traps were not deployed for the detection of D. citri, as there was no requirement or recommendation to do so.

citations.text: Where the pest is found to be present, operators are instructed to implement increased frequency of pesticide applications by spraying for the control of S. frugiperda. According to the CA, at the stage when larvae were detected, it was largely ineffective due to inappropriate timing of applications as the caterpillar was already protected in the plant. According to the CA, the option of burning of the crops is not possible during the hot summer months due to the risk of wildfires.

The EFSA pest risk assessment for S. frugiperda (section 4.2)7 states that "if this pest were to arrive and become a pest of maize in Europe, it is likely that the existing available tools could be used to control it effectively". However, the CA has not defined official procedures for treatment against the pest (see paragraph 13). Treatment methods, such as the use of chemical pesticides at other growth stages (flight season of adult moths, young larvae stages), the use of biological control agents, destruction or deep burial of infested material and other host plants, burning of plant material in other seasons, soil cultivation, have not been assessed or defined as official treatment procedures by the CA. This is not in line with Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, which requires the CA to immediately take all the necessary phytosanitary measures for the eradication of the pest, and Article 9(a) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134, which requires appropriate treatments against the specified pest, in all the stages of its development, where the migratory nature of the adult pests, the distribution of host plants and the feeding habits of its larvae shall be considered. Point 14, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and ISPM 5 defines treatment as an "official or non-official procedure for the killing, inactivation or removal of pests, or for rendering pests infertile or for devitalization".

Operators are advised that the movement of the upper layer of soil from infested plots is prohibited and they are to apply strict hygiene measures with regards to the movement of machinery and equipment in and out of infested areas. However, the implementation of these measures is not supervised or verified by the CA.

Furthermore, the CA have not introduced restrictions on the cultivation, harvesting or movement of possibly infested plant material from infested plots. Maize cobs for human consumption and plant material for animal feed are permitted to move out of these infested plots and are traded all over Cyprus.

Risk management measures targeting prevention and elimination of infestation are outlined in Annex II, section 1 point 1 (b) and (c) to Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 as provided for in Article 17(1) in the same Regulation. This provides for measures regarding restrictions on the cultivation and use of the infested plants and movement of machinery in order to limit the spread of the pest. Furthermore, EPPO standard on guidelines on the design and implementation of a bufferzone (PM 5/10), recommends to restrict the spread of the pest by preventing the movement out of the infested area and buffer zone. 7 EFSA PRA Spodoptera.pdf 15 5.5.2 Measures for eradication of Diaphorina citri

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure the effectiveness, appropriateness, qual- ity and consistency of official controls when verifying operators and products compliance with applicable legal requirements in the fishery sector in line with Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The VS has an internal audit system, and the fishery sector was covered in 2013. The VS monitors the implementation of the official control plans by receiving the completed checklists and the DVOs' reports every six and twelve months. When serious non- compliances at operators are detected, joint inspections can be carried out, but in these cases, evaluation of the performance of the individual officers is not included. The aforementioned tools are not adequate to allow the CA to have an overview of the effectiveness and appropriateness of the controls as set out in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Additionally, the VS does not have in place control verification procedures in line with Article 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on competent authorities

The lack of verification mechanism leaves the VS unaware of the real effectiveness and appropriateness of controls carried out and the compliance level of operators in the fishery sector as identified, among other things, during the previous DG SANTE audits on the same topic.

The audit team reviewed the approvals of several on-land establishments and noted that in general the procedure described above was followed. However, the timelines between conditional and final approvals were not always respected and exceeded a total of six months. This is not in line with Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team noted that when new premises were built to replace the old one, in the same location with the same activity, there was not a new approval carried out. According to the CA, the current national approval procedure is not clear in this kind of case.

The procedure described above is not in line with Article 148(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires that after three months, the CA must either extend the conditional approval (for a period not exceeding a total of six months) or issue a final approval. The exception (i.e. the possibility to extend conditional approval to a total of 12 months) applies only to factory and freezer vessels.

The audit team noted that even the current procedure is not always followed with regard to the deadlines set: one of the RVs was conditionally approved in 2020 and has not yet been granted with a final approval.

The procedures adopted to approve operators are broadly in line with the applicable EU legislation, except for RVs. Additionally, the timelines related to conditional approvals are not always respected and may be extended beyond the deadlines foreseen in EU rules allowing operators to carry out activities without not meeting all requirements.

The audit team carried out a desk-based assessment of the documented controls over RVs. The planned inspection frequency has not been respected and was consequently extended to six years instead of four years. The audit team noted that HACCP plans did not cover all relevant areas e.g. temperatures in the holds and fishery product traceability.

HACCP-based procedures are assessed by the central level at the time of approval. The DVO officials explained that they only check recordings and sampling by the operator related to HACCP and they do not review the HACCP plans themselves during inspections. Consequently, none of the reports included remarks of any non-compliances 9 in the operators' HACCP plans (see findings in paragraphs 49 and 50 on HACCP non- compliances).

The audit team noted that in many cases the operators had used external consultants to produce their HACCP plans. When reviewing the plans, the audit team noted discrepancies in relation to current processes and EU legislation. Furthermore, the HACCP plans were not always updated, when changes in activities and/or equipment occurred.

The audit team noted that in many cases HACCP hazard analysis did not include all possible hazards (no physical and chemical hazards included), critical control points had critical limits (temperatures) not in line with EU rules, monitoring of critical limits was not adequately determined, and in case of failures to comply with a critical limit (mainly related to temperatures of frozen fishery products), adequate corrective actions were not defined properly. When questioned, the operators did not have knowledge and ownership over their HACCP plans.

In addition to the findings related to HACCP-based procedures, the audit team noted non- compliances in many other areas, which were either not covered during official controls or, if checked, non-compliances were not detected and/or not recorded in the reports (see below paragraphs 52 - 59). The audit team did not find any evidence of enforcement measures used as defined in Articles 137 and 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. When questioned, the officials explained that due to the good cooperation with the operators, and because the use of enforcement measures is too much workload and time consuming, there has not been willingness to take measures. Unfortunately, many of the findings in this report are a repetition of the findings made during the previous DG SANTE audits in Cyprus for fishery products showing that the official control system has systematically failed to adequately implement official controls contrary to requirements in Article 5(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Regarding non-compliances in the cold chain, the audit team noted the following during the visits: storage temperature records for chambers with frozen fishery products showed consistently temperatures above -18, temperature recording devices were not in place, not properly recording or not in a place where it can be easily read, locations of temperature sensors were unknown or not situated in the area of the highest temperature, temperatures measured from frozen fishery products were above the EU limits (starting from -12) and cold chambers with products stored up to the doors preventing access and proper air circulation. Those non compliances were not identified by the operators and the officials during inspections.

Freezing of fishery products was carried out for whole wrapped fish, such as tuna, in a cold store with no criteria for rapid freezing and/or controlling the freezing process. In another case, fishery products frozen two weeks ago were found to have a core temperature of -12, while the temperature recording display showed -23 (at the time of the visit the blast freezer was used as a storage facility for polystyrene boxes). 10

Significant non-compliances in general hygiene were noted in areas where chilled fresh fish was processed as well as the excessive use of water resulting in spillage to floor instead of being directing to a drain. The audit team noted condensation above unprotected fishery products. In one case, bins used for the transport of farmed fish were dirty and had a bad odour as they were only flushed briefly after use and then stored outside at high ambient temperature waiting to be washed later before use. These bins (washed and filled with some ice), were still dirty. Officials were unaware of this situation.

Maintenance issues, some significant, were detected in several premises. In some cases, it was explained to the audit team that verbal orders have been given, and some corrective actions had been taken by the operators.
Deficiencies in pest control were noted due to the gaps around doors and fans. Live ants and flies were detected in some establishments.

Traceability was not ensured when fishery products were found in cold storage without any labels. During one traceability exercise, the operator was not able to show evidence of the origin of the raw material.

Hygiene of water was not ensured when seawater, added to bins with ice, was taken from the dock. In addition, the ice machine checked by the audit team was rusty, the room had dirty walls and ceiling and the process of loading ice into transport bins was unhygienic. In another case, the water treatment system with an ultraviolet lamp for river water had not been maintained since 2010. In addition, the analysis did not include all relevant chemical parameters.

The audit team identified non-compliances on the labelling of fishery products with regard to identification marking, mandatory information of origin, references to aquaculture/wild catch, latin names of species, storage temperatures, and when relevant, a warning on potential gastrointestinal effects of consuming oilfish (Ruvettus pretiosus). Conclusions on official controls on the production and placing on the market

Official controls as implemented are not identifying and/or recording a range of readily apparent non-compliances in HACCP based plans, maintenance, hygiene, cold chain, pest control, traceability and labelling. Additionally, when non-compliances are detected, the CA is reluctant to use enforcement measures.

In the absence of on-the-spot verification of officials' performance when carrying out official controls, the VS is not aware of the situation described above, and that official 11 controls, as systematically inadequately implemented, cannot ensure the compliance of operators and processing of fishery products with food safety requirements as already noted during the previous DG SANTE audits on the same topic. 5.3.2 Official controls of fishery products Legal requirements Council Regulation (EC) No 2406/96. recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that landing sites and primary production fishing vessels below 12 meters in length are included in risk-based controls in line with Article 67(a) and (b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: Vessels below 12 meters in length belonging to categories A and B are currently not included in the annual control plans. This is not in line with Article 67(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The VS informed the audit team that they have been excluded 8 from the controls mainly due to lack of resources, difficulty to reach the vessels and they do not need a certificate of compliance to operate. The VS added that they can be inspected on a random basis, if available and if an inspection to a landing site takes place (see paragraph 43). During an on-site visit to one landing site, two such vessels came back from a fishing trip. The DVO official inspected these vessels and detected the same non- compliances noted by the audit team (the reuse of polystyrene boxes, insufficient amount of ice, lack of cleanliness and absence of protection from the sun).

Based on information provided, controls of landing sites have not been planned and consequently not carried out since 2020. This is not in line with Article 67(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The official control system covers land-based establishments, aquaculture farms and to some extent, RVs and primary production fishing vessels above 12 meters in length. Official controls are performed using documented procedures covering the required aspects. However, landing sites and primary production fishing vessels below 12 meters in length are omitted from the official control planning and, thus a significant proportion of the production chain is not subject to official controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the NRL operates and is accredited in accordance with the standard EN ISO/IEC 17025, in line with Article 100(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusion No: 15.

citations.text: This Law empowers inspectors from the LCS to access any property, including private property, for the implementation of the measures listed in the paragraph above. Access can only be granted following the consent of the owner, according to the Constitution of the Republic of Cyprus. The Plant Protection Laboratory (PPL) has been officially designated by the CA as the national reference laboratory for plant health in Cyprus. recommendations.text: Ensure that surveys on D. ciliatus are risk-based, carried out in all appropriate locations, in particular non-commercial growers and wild plants of squirting cucumber, and based on sound scientific and technical principles, in line with Article 22 (1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Recommendation is based upon conclusions Nos: 19, and 33.

citations.text: In chapter 14 of the action plan, it establishes for the survey of the pest free areas (PFAs), that a sample from five to ten non-adjacent plots of main host plants per municipality/community outside of the DAs shall be taken by each of the LCS and ADO offices. Chapter 15 of the action plan details that in each plot, surveillance shall consist of the visual examination of 10 to 20% of the plants selected in a "zig-zag" pattern. This procedure does not consider surveillance in commercial operators of secondary host plants, non-agricultural plant species (in particular on squirting cucumber plants), nor in non-commercial plots (family orchards), contrary to European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recommendations for detection surveys for non-EU Tephritidae3 (see paragraph 29). This is not in line with Article 22(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 that requires that surveys on Union quarantine pests shall be risk-based, carried out in all appropriate locations used by professional operators and other persons, and based on sound scientific and technical principles. Conclusion on the action plan

Following this initial demarcation, the audit team was informed by LCS and ADO officers that they survey other professional operators in the BZ which was demarcated as the area within 2km distance from this initial IZ. The extent of demarcation for this BZ is in line with the pathways for movement of D. ciliatus as published on the EPPO website4. It is also appropriate in view of the risk of the pest spreading out of the infested zone, in line with Article 18(3) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. However, survey activities were carried out neither on non-commercial growers nor on wild plants of squirting cucumber, in most cases. Therefore, the implementation of the delimiting survey is not in line with Article 22 (1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 which requires that surveys shall be risk-based, carried out in all appropriate locations used by professional operators and other persons, and based on sound scientific and technical principles.

According to the information reported by the CA during the remote meetings of the audit, the total area surveyed in 2024 for the main four host plants were 62.78 ha of which, the presence of D. ciliatus was detected in 25.76 ha. The area surveyed, compared to the average area planted with main host plants (see section 4.3, Table 1), represent less than 10% of the area occupied by cultivated main host of D. ciliatus (see paragraph 29). The CA did not have reliable data on the secondary and wild hosts area surveyed (See paragraph 27). This is not in line with Article 22(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see paragraphs 18 and 21).

recommendations.text: Ensure that in line with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031: a. demarcated areas are immediately established, as required by Article 18(1), b. upon finding the presence of D. ciliatus in the buffer zone or in PFAs, the CA immediately notifies the Commission and the other MS, as required by Article 19 (2), and c. contact points update the notifications as soon as they have verified any relevant new information that has been made available to them, in line with Article 31(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. During the field assessments, staff from Ammochostos ADO and LCS informed the PHMSAPS that in this district, about 95% of main host producers and many secondary host plots were surveyed during the 2024 season. In the Larnaca District, officials from the ADO and LCS units informed the audit team that out of the five cultivation cycles of cucumbers per year, between two and three of these cycles per professional growers were surveyed in 2024. Officials also implemented some surveys on secondary host crops (see section 4.6) when present in the same professional operator farm.

During discussions between the LCS and ADO in the districts of Ammochostos, Larnaca and Limassol, the audit team verified that some of this information was kept in field books and not uploaded timely during the 2024 season. In the case of Ammochostos district, some of this information was reported by the LCS official to the PHMSAPS office by phone and not transferred to the spread sheets of the CA until the end of the audit (see paragraph 29). These delays in the survey data reporting represent weaknesses in the coordination and cooperation between the Units of the CA. Furthermore, this 9 practice is not in line with the requirements of point 12 (IV) of the action plan against D. ciliatus. The action plan requires that the results of the surveys and trap catches shall be uploaded by the LCS liaison offices on spread sheets located on the IT servers of the PHMSAPS. This task shall be completed before the end of the following working day (see paragraph 13, verification of procedures). This is not in line with Article 5(1)(a) and (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which, requires that when more than one unit is competent to perform official controls or other official activities, eefficient and effective coordination and cooperation shall be ensured between the different units within a CA.
This lack of up-to-date information concerning the surveys has a strong impact on the capacity of the CA to to immediately communicate the DAs to the Commission and MS.

By the end of the audit and based on the survey information collected by the district Units during 2024, the CA provided the audit team with updated information on the area surveyed for the main host plants during this year. In accordance with this latest information provided by the LCSs, the overall area surveyed of main host plants of D. ciliatus during 2024 was approximately 190 ha, which is equivalent to one quarter of the total area planted with main host crops in 2023 (see section 4.1, table 1). Of this area, D. ciliatus was found in approximately one third of this area (63.8 ha). This data significantly differs from the data reported in update number two of 10 March for Europhyt Outbreak 26245 where, the infested area reported was 25,765 ha. This is neither in line with the immediate establishment of DA as required by Article 18(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 nor Article 19 (2) of the same which, requires that upon finding the presence of the pest in the buffer zone, the MS concerned shall immediately notify the Commission and the other MS. This practice is not in line either with Article 31(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1715 which, requires that contact points shall update the notifications as soon as they have verified any relevant new information that has been made available to them.

According to the EFSA pest survey card6 for Tephritidae, detection surveys should focus mainly on Cucurbitaceae and Solanaceae cultivated as commercial crops and found as ornamentals or cultivated non-commercially in residential areas. Delimiting surveys following a detection could include all Cucurbitaceae and Solanaceae and all other species described as hosts for the detected species, that are found in the surveyed area as crops, ornamentals or naturally occurring wild plants.

recommendations.text: To ensure that comparative assessments are conducted for the authorisation of PPPs containing active substances that are candidates for substitution. This is to comply with Articles 50(4) of Regulation (EC) No. 1107/2009.

citations.text: In cases where PPPs contain candidates for substitution, the CA does not perform comparative assessments, relying instead on evaluations conducted by the MS that authorised the reference PPP product. The audit team expressed concerns that relying on the other MS evaluation is not correct, as safer, equally suitable alternatives may be available in Cyprus, that were not available in the MS that conducted the evaluation. The fact that the CA does not consider performing the comparative assessments, even at the renewal phase, is not in line with article 50(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009.

However, the authorisation process does not include conducting comparative assessments for PPPs that contain candidates for substitution against alternatives with potentially safer active substances, and emergency authorisations are not immediately notified to the Commission and MSs.

recommendations.text: To ensure that emergency authorisations are immediately notified to the Com- mission and Member States. This is to comply with Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No. 1107/2009.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the frequency of inspections at operators is decided upon using objective criteria that consider the risk of inappropriate PPP usage and the results of monitoring programmes as necessary. This is to comply with Article 9(1) and 24(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions Nos 55 and 56.

citations.text: Re-packaging activities may involve PPPs imported from non-EU countries for re-export or PPPs from other EU MSs marketed in Cyprus under parallel-trade permits. The CA considers parallel trade a high-risk activity and requires distributors to obtain approval for each movement of PPPs. Additionally, distributors must notify the CA at least three days in advance of any intended re-packaging. The audit team considered this a good practice, as it provides insight into the volume of products entering the Cypriot market and the proportion subject to re-packaging. However, at the time of the audit, this information was not being used to plan controls for re-packaging operators. The absence of regular inspections for an activity considered high-risk is not in accordance with Articles 9(1) and 11 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Planning of official controls on use of PPPs

The results from previous inspections and samples collected by LCS inspectors serve to identify the high-risk crops for the upcoming year's inspection planning. However, there is no specific criteria for selecting operators who grow these high-risk crops, leading to a random selection process. This approach does not fully comply with Articles 9(1) and 24(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Moreover, with the low number of inspections, it becomes more important to target operators who may pose the higher risk.

The results of the national pesticide residue programme mentioned in paragraph 27 are not taken into account for the planning of inspections. This is not in line with Article 24(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team considered that the results that show exceedance of maximum residue levels for authorised PPPs would be relevant for follow-up during inspections, as growers might have either use an excessive amount of PPPs or applied them too close to harvest. Results showing unauthorised use of PPPs are taken into account for the sampling programme, see below.

The relatively high non-compliance rate of samples taken by the LCS (18 out of 79 in 2024) compared to favourable results from formulation analysis (see paragraph 51) suggests that there is a higher risk associated with the misuse of authorised products by growers or the use of illegally traded PPPs (see paragraph 26) than with the marketing of unauthorised PPPs. This is not adequately considered by the CAs when determining the number of inspections at growers, which is significantly less representative than the number carried out at market level.

recommendations.text: To define conditions and establish criteria for when prior notice to agricultural users would be necessary and duly justified for the official controls to be carried out. This is to comply with Article 9 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: While market operator inspections are generally conducted unannounced, all grower inspections are announced, with growers receiving 3-4 days' notice. The DoA stated that this advance notice is necessary, as growers are often not present on farms. Yet, the audit team found no evidence in the inspection reports to support this necessity, and the CA confirmed that announcements are standard practice rather than exceptions. This is inconsistent with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Moreover, advance notice could compromise inspection effectiveness by allowing operators ample time to alter conditions at their premises, such as removing unauthorised PPPs. Planning of sampling for formulation analyses of PPPs

Official controls at market level are carried out unannounced. However, prior notice is given to growers in all cases, with no justified reason, and long time in advance. This undermines the effectiveness of the inspections.

recommendations.text: To define and implement measures and criteria for the withdrawal of training certificates provided to users, distributors and advisors. This is to comply with Article 5(2) of Directive 2008/128/EC.

citations.text: The national legislation includes provisions for the potential withdrawal of certificates. However, at the time of the audit, no procedures were defined for the conditions under which certificates might be withdrawn, and no certificates had yet been withdrawn since the system's implementation. This lack of defined procedures is not in compliance with Article 5(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC, which mandates that certification include criteria and processes for granting, renewing, and withdrawing certificates. Planning of official controls on marketing and distribution of PPPs

There is a certification system implemented to provide training to users, distributors and advisors that overall works well. However, there are no measures foreseen for the withdrawal of certificates as necessary. 5.2.3. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure the reliability and relevance of PPP analyses, and in particular that: - - The laboratory conducting the analysis is accredited to ISO/IEC 17025. - - Samples of PPPs are analysed to determine the presence of unacceptable co- formulants set out in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and the con- tent of impurities whose maximum content is established in the approval of rele- vant active substances, as referred to Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. This is to comply with Articles 37(4)(e) and 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions No 65.

citations.text: However, at the time of the audit, the laboratory had not yet been accredited to ISO/IEC 17025, which according to article 37(1) and 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 is a requirement for the designation of laboratories to carry out analysis of samples of goods taken during official controls.

Furthermore, the laboratory's analysis focuses solely on active substances, without considering unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities. This prevents the CA from fully complying with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA noted that currently, there are accredited methods for only a few impurities, and this poses a 14 common challenge across all Member States, suggesting that this issue requires discussion and resolution at EU level. Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls

recommendations.text: To ensure the quality, consistency and effectiveness of official controls, in par- ticular that: - - Information and checklists provided to inspectors cover the verification of all relevant aspects of compliance of operators with articles 55, 65 and 67 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. - - There is supervision of the inspectors, to identify and correct any weakness- es in their performance. This is to comply with Articles 4(2)(a), 5 (1)(a) and (b), 12(1) and 14(b)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusions Nos 33,34, 85 and 97. to 75 and 89 to 93.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the primary aim of inspections, both at market and user levels, is to verify basic compliance aspects without further thorough verification (see paragraphs 70, 73 and 90). These weaknesses had not been detected by the central CA, as there was no supervision of inspectors' work at the time of this audit. This oversight deficiency does not comply with Articles 5(1) (a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA indicated that a recent internal audit identified this issue and announced plans to initiate supervision activities shortly. Conclusions on the competent authorities

As described in paragraph 42, at the time of the audit, re-packers were not subject to regular inspections. As part of the audit, a visit was made to a re-packer of PPPs for demonstration purposes, allowing the CA to discuss with the audit team the key areas inspectors would focus on during their inspections. The audit team noted that the checklist designed for inspecting this activity generally provides sufficient guidance for ensuring compliance with relevant legislation. However, some aspects, such as the process inspectors should follow to verify the source and quantities of PPPs through invoices, or whether they need to take samples, may require further clarification.

The audit team noted that the checklist used for this inspection contained only one point related to the control of PPPs, specifically the verification of input/output flow. All other checklist items pertained to structural and storage conditions. Inspectors are not required to verify whether the purchased and stored PPPs were authorised or whether operators maintain records of these products for at least five years. The checklist also lacked items related to verifying stocks or ensuring that stored PPPs were labelled in accordance with their authorised conditions. This lack of comprehensive guidance for inspections is not in line with Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Additionally, the failure to verify these compliance aspects contravenes Articles 14(b)(i), (ii), (iv), and (e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, as well as Articles 65 and 67 of Regulation (EC) No. 1107/2009. Controls at retailers of PPPs

The audit team noted that the basic checks done during the inspections where no samples are taken, are often ineffective in identifying non-compliance issues such as incorrect labelling. For example, inspectors failed to notice errors on the labels of two PPPs. One product´s label lacked usage instructions, while the other, in some packages, had unclear or missing instructions related to a recent restriction of usage only in greenhouses. These superficial checks are not sufficient as to meet the requirement of article 14 (b)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and to verify that the PPPs labels meet the requirement of Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No. 1107/2009.
